Neural population activity for memory: Properties, computations, and codes

Silences, spikes and bursts: Three-part knot of the neural code

Rate Coding and temporal coding

Rate coding

Information encoded in firing rates averaged over time windows ( 50-500ms) A 2025 computational study compares spike-timing codes (Figure) 41. The model tests how convergence affects temporal coding (Figure).

Robust to noise but limited temporal precision

Often associated with the intensity of a stimulus or the strength of a represented feature

Most common in cortical areas for stable feature representation

Energy-efficient for sustained representations

Temporal Coding

Information in precise spike timing, not just the rate

Includes spike synchrony, phase-of-firing (e.g., relative to neural oscillations like theta or gamma), and specific inter-spike intervals

Phase-of-firing coding: spikes locked to oscillatory phases (theta, gamma); synchronized circuits

Spike timing dependent plasticity (STDP) suggests temporal precision matters

Population Coding and Cell Assemblies

Noisy single neurons become reliable when pooled across tens-thousands of cells. Population-vector and probabilistic-population-code formalisms describe how stimulus features reside in the geometry of ensemble activity, while Hebbian plasticity binds repeatedly co-active neurons into enduring "cell assemblies" that can later be reactivated during recall or planning, supporting attractor dynamics, error correction, and pattern completion

Basis for most modern decoding approaches

Sparse vs distributed representations

Overall: only  1-5% of neurons active at any given time, enabling high representational capacity while minimizing metabolic costs and interference

Early sensory areas favour dense codes that maximise fidelity under wiring constraints, whereas hippocampal and higher association areas adopt sparse codes (<5%<5\% of neurons active at a time) that minimise interference between memories, facilitate pattern separation, and economise metabolic cost. A 2025 computational model relates learning to cortical layers (Figure) 42. The model compares population sparseness across layers (Figure).

Biological systems span five orders of magnitude in coding density, trading energy cost for noise robustness, generalization, and rapid readout

Enables smooth generalization

The degree of sparsity also depends on how novel a stimulus is; novel stimuli will have sparser codes due to less resonance with the existing conceptual mesh, which is mitigated through gradual integration

Neuromodulators control sparsity:

During states of focused attention and waking exploration, cholinergic input from the medial septum raises the threshold for recurrent excitation within CA3 and CA1 networks. This heightened threshold reduces the likelihood that overlapping populations of place cells fire together, enforcing a sparse code that’s ideal for encoding new spatial experiences. Conversely, when acetylcholine levels drop during slow-wave sleep, CA3 recurrent collaterals become more excitable, promoting dense, synchronized bursts (sharp-wave ripples) that facilitate memory consolidation. In essence, acetylcholine dynamically gates the transition between dense replay (sleep) and sparse encoding (wake), controlling how many neurons coactivate and thus modulating representational sparsity on the order of seconds to minutes.

Dopamine, too, exerts control over sparsity, particularly in the prefrontal cortex and striatal circuits. By binding to D1 versus D2 receptors, dopamine shifts the balance between excitatory pyramidal neurons and inhibitory interneurons, adjusting overall network gain. Under high-dopamine conditions-such as during reward anticipation-prefrontal neurons adopt a higher excitability state but also sharpen their tuning curves, meaning each neuron responds more selectively to its preferred input. That selective tuning yields a sparse code: fewer neurons respond strongly to particular task-relevant cues, bolstering signal-to-noise and improving working memory robustness. When dopamine levels drop, tuning broadens, allowing a denser ensemble to participate but at the cost of decreased selectivity. Thus, dopamine dynamically alters sparsity to match behavioral demands-tight, sparse representations during high-reward or high-attention situations, and more distributed representations when flexibility is needed.

The neocortex implements various attractor types:

Point attractors: Stable memories, categorical decisions

Line/ring attractors: Working memory, head direction

Chaotic attractors: Flexible computation, exploration

Oscillations and phase locking

Resonant hierarchies: a multiscale framework for oscillatory dynamics in the brain

Oscillatory control of cortical space as a computational dimension

Cortical traveling waves in time and space

The neocortex exhibits rhythmic activity at multiple frequencies:

Gamma (30-100 Hz): Local computation, attention, binding

Beta (12-30 Hz): Motor control, status quo maintenance

Alpha (8-12 Hz): Inhibition, sensory gating

Theta (4-8 Hz): Memory encoding, navigation

Delta (0.5-4 Hz): Sleep, long-range coordination

These aren’t noise-they serve functional roles in:

Gating information flow between regions

Temporal binding of distributed representations

Multiplexing multiple computations

Memory consolidation during sleep

Definitions and functions

Neural oscillations are rhythmic fluctuations of neural activity, occurring across a wide range of frequencies. Classic electrophysiology defines bands such as delta (∼0-4Hz), theta (∼4-8Hz), alpha (∼8-12Hz), beta (∼12-30Hz), and gamma (>30Hz) 8. These oscillatory patterns are observed at multiple scales - from local field potentials to EEG - effectively bridging micro-level neuron spiking and macro-level brain dynamics 9. Far from being mere epiphenomena, oscillations are increasingly recognized as playing integral roles in brain function. Mechanistically, they stem from circuit interactions (e.g. recurrent excitation/inhibition loops) that produce rhythmic cycles of neural excitability. In essence, oscillations modulate when neurons are closer to or farther from firing threshold, creating repeating windows of high and low spiking probability. This means oscillatory phase is deeply tied to neuronal excitability: "they move the membrane potential towards and away from the spiking threshold." 10. In other words, oscillations provide a temporal scaffolding that organizes neural firing in time. Beyond shifting single-cell excitability, population rhythms create spatially patterned electric fields that coordinate large ensembles almost instantaneously, aligning windows of high gain across millimeters of cortex-an emergent property not reducible to individual spikes 11. A human-connectome study examines structure relevant to traveling waves (Figure). The study simulates traveling waves on a human cortical network (Figure).

Phase locking refers to the synchronization of oscillation phase across different neurons or regions - effectively aligning their high-excitability periods. This synchronization is thought to be crucial for communication in neural networks. According to the "communication through coherence" hypothesis, coherent oscillations enable selective information routing: inputs arriving at a target area’s excitable phase (i.e. when its oscillation is at the optimal phase) are transmitted most effectively 12. For two neural groups to exchange signals reliably, their oscillations must be appropriately phase-locked so that spikes from the sender arrive during the receiver’s peak excitability. Empirical evidence strongly supports this idea. For example, synchronized gamma-band oscillations between visual cortex areas V1 and V4 have been shown to improve visual processing - when the two areas’ gamma rhythms are in phase prior to a stimulus change, animals detect the change faster, whereas misaligned phases correlate with slower reaction times 13. This suggests that inter-area phase alignment gates effective connectivity: coherence does not just time when signals pass; alpha/beta coherence also sculpts where they can pass. Under the "spatial computing" paradigm, top-down control is implemented as spatial patterns of alpha/beta that transiently veto or permit local gamma bursts, effectively laying a stencil over cortex so only selected columns express content during their optimal phase. This converts cortical space itself into a computational dimension for selective routing and gating 14, 6, 11. High coherence between brain regions often predicts better performance on cognitive tasks, consistent with the view that oscillatory phase locking underlies attention and neural communication.

Neural oscillations also contribute to how information is represented and grouped in the brain. A prominent example is feature binding in perception: neurons encoding different features of the same object can oscillate in synchrony (particularly in the gamma range), effectively "tagging" those features as belonging together. Classic studies found that neurons in visual cortex synchronize their gamma oscillations when an animal perceives a coherent object, suggesting gamma synchrony is a mechanism for binding distributed features into one percept 8. In practice, feature binding rides on where alpha/beta releases cortical patches from suppression; the spatial pattern of that release determines which assemblies can synchronize in gamma at a given moment 11.

Oscillatory timing may also help segregate distinct representations: by assigning different phases or frequencies to different information streams, the brain can avoid interference between concurrent signals. In the prefrontal cortex, for instance, neurons have been observed to use phase-specific firing to encode multiple items in working memory. In primate PFC, information about multiple items is time-division multiplexed: item-specific spikes ride on distinct gamma bursts locked to different phases of a slower carrier, while intermittent beta bursts gate which cortical patches are allowed to express those gamma packets 15. The first item’s spikes were concentrated at an earlier phase of the cycle and the second item at a later phase, implying a phase-of-firing code that multiplexed two memory representations without confusion. By oscillatory phase-locking of spikes, the brain can thus disambiguate multiple pieces of information held at once. This principle - using oscillation phase as an extra coding dimension - appears to be widespread, allowing temporal ordering of spikes to signal different content even if average firing rates are similar. This regime enables rapid remapping by changing the spatial pattern of beta without relearning the content itself.

Oscillations across different frequency bands often interact to support complex cognitive operations. Cross-frequency coupling provides a way to link fast, local processes with slower, broad coordination. In the hippocampus and cortex, for example, high-frequency gamma bursts (which accompany local neuronal ensembles firing) are often nested within slower theta oscillation cycles 16. The slower rhythm (theta,  6-8Hz) can modulate the amplitude or timing of the faster gamma, effectively organizing sequential neural firing within each theta cycle (a phenomenon important for episodic memory encoding) 16. Such theta-gamma coupling is hypothesized to underlie the neural coding of sequences - e.g. during navigation, successive places along a route may be activated on successive gamma sub-cycles of each theta wave (more on this later!). More broadly, many brain regions share a common set of rhythms (delta, theta, gamma) that appear during specific behavioral states to orchestrate memory operations 16. During active wakefulness (and REM sleep), the "fast" mode of network oscillations emerges: hippocampal and cortical circuits engage theta and gamma rhythms which are associated with effective encoding and retrieval of memories. By contrast, in slow-wave sleep the brain switches to a "slow" oscillatory mode (dominant delta waves and sporadic bursts) that supports memory consolidation. In all cases, oscillations serve as a timing infrastructure to coordinate memory systems - they constrain when neurons fire and thereby help organize the flow of information for encoding, consolidation, or recall. Notably, gamma oscillations are found in hippocampus, cortex, and striatum alike, where they compress neural spiking into brief bursts, while slower oscillations (theta, delta) modulate these bursts and align activity across regions.

In summary, oscillations and phase locking appear to be fundamental organizational principles of the brain’s computations. By synchronizing neuronal activity in time, oscillations enable efficient communication, selection, and integration of information across neural circuits. Synchronized rhythms can flexibly route signals between regions (by opening and closing communication channels via phase alignment) 12. They can group neurons into coherently firing assemblies that represent perceptual objects or memories, and can segregate different assemblies by assigning them different phases or frequencies. Oscillatory timing thus provides a multiplexing scheme for the brain’s encoding of information, adding a layer of temporal coding on top of average firing rates.

How rhythms arise from circuit motifs, intrinsic cellular physics, and neuromodulation

At the microcircuit level, the most ubiquitous generator of cortical rhythm is the excitatory-inhibitory loop. In PING (pyramidal-interneuron gamma), local excitation transiently drives fast-spiking PV+ interneurons; the resulting perisomatic GABAA inhibition silences the population and, as it decays, the cycle repeats. In ING (interneuron-network gamma), mutually coupled interneurons (helped by gap junctions) can oscillate with minimal excitatory drive. The dominant clock in both cases is set by synaptic kinetics and delays: the decay time of GABAA currents ( 6-12 ms in vivo) plus axonal/dendritic conduction times places the natural frequency in the  30-90 Hz gamma range, while slower inhibition (GABAB), NMDA currents, and longer loops push networks toward beta/alpha. Stronger tonic excitation typically raises gamma frequency and lowers its power; weaker drive does the opposite-classic PING behavior. These principles, worked out in theory and slice/optogenetic work, now anchor most mechanistic accounts of fast rhythms 17, 18, 19, 20.

Perisomatic PV+ inhibition gives gamma its precision, but electrical coupling between interneurons further boosts phase-locking and speed. PV-basket cells and chandelier cells are richly coupled by connexin-36 gap junctions; blocking these junctions degrades interneuron synchrony and weakens fast oscillations. In hippocampus, the sharp-wave ripple ( 140-200 Hz) exemplifies an extreme: tightly timed recurrent inhibition among PV basket cells can pace pyramidal populations at ripple frequencies; cutting PV-PV connections or perturbing their GABAA time constant desynchronizes the ripple 21, 22, 23.

Rhythmogenesis is not only a network property; single-cell intrinsic dynamics supply resonant preferences and rebound mechanisms that circuits recruit. Subthreshold membrane resonance arises when restorative currents (notably Ih and M-current IM) counteract capacitive lag, endowing neurons with band-pass impedance that peaks in theta-alpha or beta ranges depending on channel densities and dendritic morphology. These same currents bias spike timing to preferred phases when the cell sits in an oscillatory field. Separately, post-inhibitory rebound-driven by T-type Ca2+ channels, often in concert with Ih-turns inhibition into precise timing pulses; this is central to thalamic bursting and to thalamocortical alpha-like rhythms. Persistent Na+ currents and dendritic Ca2+ conductances can sustain or amplify subthreshold oscillations, further shaping local frequency content 24, 25, 26, 27, 28.

Specific long-range motifs favor particular bands. The septohippocampal loop (GABAergic and cholinergic neurons in medial septum entraining hippocampal interneurons and pyramids) acts as a theta-rate metronome; cooling the septum slows hippocampal theta with preserved phase lags, consistent with a pacemaker/organizer role 29. Thalamocortical circuits, with low-threshold Ca2+ spikes in thalamic relay cells and inhibitory gating from the thalamic reticular nucleus, readily generate alpha and spindles and impose phasic inhibition onto cortex 30. Cortico-basal-ganglia-thalamic loops naturally express beta, especially under dopaminergic control; in sensorimotor systems, beta power/coherence scales with maintenance or withholding of action and can become pathologically exaggerated in Parkinsonism 31.

Cortex itself is spectrally laminated. Superficial layers tend to express gamma (driven by feedforward input and PING-like microcircuits), whereas deep layers favor alpha-beta that broadcast feedback predictions and top-down control. Models and laminar recordings show deep-layer alpha/beta phasically suppress superficial gamma/spiking, yielding a multiplexed channel 32, 33, 34.

Beyond zero-lag synchrony, anatomical delays and spatial coupling make rhythms travel. Alpha, theta, and beta often propagate as traveling waves across cortex, sequencing distant columns by phase and turning space into a timing dimension for routing 35, 36. Connectome-constrained models and ECoG show that structural gradients steer wave direction and speed; in behaving primates, beta traveling waves in frontoparietal networks track recent reward history and working-memory demands 37. In effect, traveling waves instantiate a spatiotemporal form of communication-through-coherence: with finite conduction delays, only particular phase offsets let inputs arrive during a target’s high-gain window, and the wave’s phase gradient supplies those offsets to open selective channels between areas. A 2026 study presents a method for detecting traveling waves (Figure) 43. The study applies the method to marmoset recordings (Figure). A 2026 preprint examines waves across macaque cortical depth (Figure) 44. The preprint proposes a mechanism linking waves and spiking (Figure).

Finally, neuromodulators retune the whole dynamical substrate. Acetylcholine suppresses Im and some intracortical inhibition, increasing excitability and biasing networks toward high-frequency packets; in hippocampus, muscarinic drive can scale gamma power and septal cholinergic input promotes theta while suppressing ripples-consistent with an encoding-mode shift 38, 39. Norepinephrine flattens low-frequency synchronization and desynchronizes cortex during arousal surges, while sustained tone sets longer-lived gain states; pupil-linked LC activity tracks these shifts 39. Dopamine in cortico-basal-ganglia loops modulates beta-band propensity and coherence, reshaping temporal control of movement and working memory 40. By dialing channel conductances and E/I balance, neuromodulators move circuits across attractor regimes-altering not only which rhythms appear but their phase relations, cross-frequency coupling, and effective connectivity.
